title: Does Pooping Help a Hangover? Why You Feel Better After You Go
excerpt: Why a bowel movement can make a hangover feel better, why it does not flush out alcohol, why drinking causes loose stools or constipation, and when bathroom trouble needs a doctor.
metaDescription: Does pooping help a hangover? Why you feel better after you go, why it does not flush out alcohol, why drinking loosens stools, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** pooping can make you feel noticeably better for a little while when you're hungover, but it doesn't flush alcohol out of your body or speed up your recovery. The relief is real. It comes from your nervous system and from emptying a gut that alcohol has irritated, not from "getting the toxins out." By the time you're hungover, almost all the alcohol you drank has already been absorbed into your blood and broken down by your liver. Your stool carries very little of it. So enjoy the relief, but don't count on the bathroom to cure the rest of the hangover. Water, food, sleep, and time are still doing the real work.

**The quick rules:** If you feel better after a bowel movement, that's normal and harmless. If you have loose stools, drink extra fluids with some salt and sugar in them, because diarrhea makes dehydration worse. Don't strain, and don't sit on the toilet for a long time if you feel dizzy or lightheaded. Don't take laxatives or drink large amounts of coffee to "force" a bowel movement to clear a hangover. It won't clear the hangover, and it can make dehydration worse.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most hangover bathroom trips are unpleasant but harmless and settle within a day. **Get medical care if** you see blood in your stool or black, tarry stools, you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe or constant belly pain, diarrhea lasts more than two days, you can't keep fluids down, or you have signs of serious dehydration such as very little urine, a racing heart, or feeling faint when you stand. **If you faint on the toilet, hit your head, or have chest pain or trouble breathing, call 911.** If you notice shaking, sweating, or anxiety that starts when you stop drinking after several days of heavy use, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which is a medical issue. Tell a doctor plainly; it's common and treatable.

## Why You Feel Better After Pooping With a Hangover

A lot of people notice that the worst of the morning-after misery lifts a bit right after a bowel movement. The nausea eases, the cramping stops, and some people even feel a wave of calm or a little lightheaded relief. There are a few overlapping reasons, and none of them involve pushing alcohol out of your body.

### 1. Your vagus nerve gets involved

The **vagus nerve** is a long nerve that runs from your brainstem down through your chest and into your gut. It's a major part of the "rest and digest" side of your nervous system, the part that slows your heart and relaxes your body.

When you have a bowel movement, especially a large one, the stretching of the rectum and the act of bearing down can stimulate the vagus nerve. That can briefly lower your heart rate and blood pressure. For many people, the result is a pleasant sense of relaxation and relief. Some gastroenterologists have nicknamed this feeling "poo-phoria," a term popularized by the book *What's Your Poo Telling You?* by Dr. Anish Sheth and Josh Richman.

When you're hungover, your body is often stuck in a stressed, jittery state. Your heart may be beating faster than normal, and many people feel anxious and on edge. A short burst of vagus nerve activity can take the edge off that for a few minutes. It's a real effect. It just isn't a treatment for the hangover itself.

### 2. An irritated gut finally settles

Alcohol irritates the lining of the stomach and intestines. After a night of drinking, your gut is often full of gas, partly digested food, and extra fluid that didn't get absorbed properly. That causes cramping, bloating, and that queasy, uneasy feeling in your belly.

Emptying the bowel removes a lot of that pressure. If your gut was cramping and bloated, a bowel movement can make it calmer almost immediately. Since a lot of hangover misery is centered in the stomach, easing it can make the whole morning feel more manageable.

### 3. Relief from waiting

There's a simpler reason too. If you've been lying in bed feeling an urgent need to go, and dreading it, getting it over with is a relief in itself. Physical discomfort and the anxiety about it both drop at once.

### 4. It often happens alongside other things that help

Many people's morning routine goes: wake up, drink water or coffee, eat something, use the bathroom. Water and food help a hangover. Coffee can perk you up. When you feel better afterward, it's easy to give the bathroom trip all the credit, even though the other parts of the routine are doing some of the work.

## Does Pooping Get Rid of Alcohol?

No, not in any meaningful way. This is the most common misunderstanding behind the question, so it's worth explaining clearly.

When you drink, alcohol is absorbed quickly through the walls of your stomach and, mostly, your small intestine. It passes into your bloodstream well before it would reach your colon, where stool is formed. By the time you wake up hungover, the alcohol has long since left your gut.

Once alcohol is in your blood, your **liver** handles the vast majority of it. It turns alcohol into a toxic compound called **acetaldehyde** and then into acetate, which your body breaks down further into carbon dioxide and water. A small fraction of alcohol leaves your body unchanged through your breath, urine, and sweat. Stool isn't a meaningful exit route.

That means:

- **You can't poop out alcohol** to sober up faster or lower your blood alcohol level.
- **You can't poop out acetaldehyde.** This compound, which is thought to contribute to hangover symptoms, is made and broken down mainly in the liver.
- **A bowel movement doesn't mean the hangover is "leaving your system."** Hangovers peak around the time your blood alcohol returns to zero, and they're driven by things like dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation, and the after-effects of alcohol on your brain and gut. None of those are fixed by a trip to the bathroom.

The only time your body clears something directly through the bowel is when it's still in your gut, such as food or fluid that wasn't absorbed. That's part of why stools after drinking are often loose.

## Why Alcohol Makes You Poop More (and Why It's Often Diarrhea)

If you've ever noticed that a night of drinking leads to urgent, frequent, or loose bowel movements the next morning (sometimes called "beer poops" or "the drunk dumps"), you're far from alone. Alcohol affects your digestive system in several ways at once. Research reviews on alcohol and the digestive tract, including a widely cited 1997 review by Christiane and J. Christian Bode in the NIAAA journal *Alcohol Health & Research World*, describe these effects.

### Alcohol changes how fast your gut moves

Alcohol affects the muscles that move food through your digestive tract. Depending on the type and amount of drink, it can make parts of the gut move faster. When food and fluid pass through your intestines too quickly, the colon doesn't have time to absorb water from it. The result is looser, more urgent stools.

### Alcohol interferes with water and nutrient absorption

The lining of your small intestine is where most nutrients and much of the water you drink is absorbed. Alcohol can irritate that lining and interfere with how it absorbs water, salts, and nutrients. When more fluid reaches the colon than it can handle, you get diarrhea.

### Alcohol irritates the gut lining

Alcohol is an irritant. Heavy drinking can inflame the lining of the stomach and intestines. That inflammation can cause cramping, urgency, and loose stools.

### What you drank matters

Your drink can make bathroom trouble worse:

- **Beer** has a lot of fluid, some carbohydrates that ferment in the gut, and carbonation, all of which can loosen stools and add gas.
- **Sugary mixers and cocktails** can pull extra water into the bowel, especially if they contain sugar alcohols or a lot of fructose.
- **Wine**, especially red, contains compounds that some people find hard on the stomach.
- **Caffeinated mixers** such as energy drinks and rum and cola add caffeine, which stimulates the colon on its own. Caffeine also masks how drunk you feel without making you any less drunk.

### The late-night food

Drinking often comes with greasy, spicy, or very large meals late at night. Fatty and spicy food can speed up the gut and cause loose stools on its own, especially when combined with alcohol. Sometimes the bathroom trouble owes as much to the 2 a.m. food as it does to the drinks.

If loose stools after drinking are a regular problem for you, our full guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) goes deeper into the causes and what helps.

## Why You Need to Go Right When You Wake Up

Many people find the urge hits within minutes of getting up, eating, or drinking coffee. That's partly the **gastrocolic reflex**, a normal reflex in which eating or drinking signals your colon to contract and make room. It's strongest in the morning. Add a gut that's already irritated and full of extra fluid from the night before, and the urge can be sudden and strong.

Coffee makes the reflex stronger for many people. A study published in the journal *Gut* in 1990 found that coffee stimulated activity in the colon in some people within minutes, and the effect wasn't only due to caffeine. That's why the morning coffee after a night out so often sends people straight to the bathroom.

## Can Pooping Make a Hangover Worse?

Sometimes, yes. The bowel movement itself is usually harmless, but a few situations deserve care.

### Diarrhea adds to dehydration

Alcohol already makes you lose fluid. It suppresses a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you urinate more while drinking. If you then have several loose stools, you lose even more water along with sodium and potassium. That can make headaches, fatigue, dizziness, and a racing heart worse.

If you have diarrhea while hungover, focus on replacing fluids and salts. Water helps, but a drink with some sodium and a little sugar helps your body absorb fluid better. Oral rehydration drinks, electrolyte drinks, broth, and salty crackers with water all work. Our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) walks through the options.

### Fainting on the toilet

The same vagus nerve effect that makes some people feel relaxed can, in a small number of people, drop their heart rate and blood pressure enough to make them faint. Doctors call this **defecation syncope** (fainting during or right after a bowel movement). It's more likely when you're dehydrated, have been drinking, get up suddenly, or strain hard.

A hangover combines several of these risk factors. To lower the risk:

- **Don't strain hard.** Let things happen at their own pace.
- **Stand up slowly** when you're done. Sit for a moment first.
- **If you feel lightheaded, sweaty, or your vision starts to gray out,** stay seated, put your head down toward your knees, and call out to someone if you can.
- **Drink some water before you go** if you're very dehydrated.

A single brief faint in a young, healthy person is often not serious, but falling can cause real injuries, especially in a bathroom with hard surfaces. If you faint and hit your head, have chest pain or a pounding, irregular heartbeat, or don't come around quickly, get emergency care. If it happens more than once, tell a doctor.

### Straining with constipation

Some people get the opposite problem and feel blocked up after drinking. Straining hard while dehydrated can trigger the same lightheaded feeling and can irritate hemorrhoids. More on that below.

## Hangover Constipation: Why Some People Can't Go

Not everyone gets diarrhea after drinking. Some people feel bloated and constipated instead. That can happen because:

- **Dehydration dries out stool.** When your body is short on water, the colon pulls more water out of stool, leaving it harder and harder to pass.
- **Sleep and routine are disrupted.** A late night, a different bedtime, and skipped meals throw off the normal timing of your gut.
- **Your diet changed.** A night of drinks and snacks often means little fiber.
- **Some medicines constipate.** Certain painkillers and other medications can slow the gut, and mixing them with alcohol can carry their own risks.

If you're constipated while hungover, drink water steadily through the day, eat something with fiber such as fruit, oatmeal, or whole grain toast, and go for a gentle walk if you feel up to it. Movement helps the gut move. Most hangover constipation settles within a day or two once you're eating and drinking normally. Avoid strong laxatives unless a doctor or pharmacist suggests one, since some types pull extra water into the bowel and can make dehydration worse.

## Should You Try to Make Yourself Poop to Cure a Hangover?

No. Since pooping doesn't remove alcohol or acetaldehyde, forcing a bowel movement won't shorten your hangover. Popular "flush it out" ideas tend to backfire:

- **Laxatives** can cause cramping, diarrhea, and more fluid and salt loss on top of what alcohol already caused.
- **Lots of strong coffee** can irritate an already upset stomach and add to anxiety and a racing heart. One cup is usually fine for regular coffee drinkers. Several cups on an empty, irritated stomach often makes things worse.
- **"Detox" teas and cleanses** often contain laxative herbs like senna. They do the same thing as laxatives, and there is no good evidence that they help a hangover.

If you need to go, go. If you don't, there's no benefit to forcing it.

## What Actually Helps a Hangover Gut

If your stomach and bowels are the worst part of your hangover, these steps are simple and supported by common sense and general medical advice:

1. **Rehydrate steadily.** Sip water and an electrolyte drink through the morning rather than chugging a large amount at once, which can upset your stomach further.
2. **Eat bland, easy food.** Toast, crackers, rice, bananas, oatmeal, broth, and eggs are gentle on the gut. Bland carbohydrates are easy to digest and help bring your blood sugar back up.
3. **Skip greasy, spicy, and very sugary food** until your gut settles. The classic greasy breakfast can make loose stools worse.
4. **Go easy on coffee.** One cup if you're used to it. Skip it if your stomach is very upset.
5. **Avoid more alcohol.** "Hair of the dog" just delays the hangover and adds more irritation to your gut.
6. **Rest.** Sleep gives your body time to recover.
7. **Be careful with painkillers.** Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate an already inflamed stomach, and acetaminophen (Tylenol) has its own liver concerns after heavy drinking. Our guides to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) and [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explain the trade-offs.

If nausea is the main problem, our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more targeted tips.

## What Your Poop Might Be Telling You After Drinking

Most changes after a night of drinking are temporary and harmless. Here's a general guide to what's common and what deserves attention.

| What you notice | What it usually means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Loose, urgent stools the morning after | Alcohol sped up your gut and reduced water absorption | Rehydrate with fluids and salts; bland food; should settle within a day |
| Dark green or unusually colored stool | Often from food coloring in drinks or mixers, or fast transit | Usually harmless; watch that it returns to normal |
| Reddish stool after red drinks | Dyes in some drinks and mixers can tint stool | Usually harmless, but if you're not sure it's dye, treat it as possible blood |
| Hard, dry stool and straining | Dehydration and low fiber | Water, fiber, gentle movement |
| Bright red blood | Can come from hemorrhoids or a small tear, but can also signal something more serious | See a doctor, especially if it's more than a streak or keeps happening |
| Black, tarry, sticky stool | Can signal bleeding higher up in the digestive tract | Get medical care promptly |
| Diarrhea lasting more than two days | May be something other than a simple hangover, such as an infection | See a doctor, and keep rehydrating |

One note on black stools: bismuth medicines such as Pepto-Bismol can temporarily turn stool black, which is harmless. If you haven't taken one and your stool is black and tarry, get checked.

## When Bathroom Trouble After Drinking Is a Warning Sign

For social drinkers, the occasional rough morning in the bathroom is unpleasant but usually nothing to worry about. A few patterns, though, are worth taking seriously:

- **Blood**, either in your stool, in vomit, or as black, tarry stools. Heavy drinking can irritate or damage the stomach lining and, less commonly, cause tears in the esophagus from repeated vomiting. These need prompt care.
- **Severe or constant belly pain**, especially pain in the upper belly that spreads to your back. This can be a sign of pancreatitis, an inflammation of the pancreas that can follow heavy drinking and needs urgent care.
- **Diarrhea that lasts more than a couple of days** or happens after almost every time you drink.
- **Signs of significant dehydration**: very little or very dark urine, dizziness when standing, a fast heartbeat, confusion, or being unable to keep fluids down.
- **Fainting**, especially if it happens more than once.

If your gut reacts badly every time you drink, even to small amounts, it's worth mentioning to a doctor. Conditions like irritable bowel syndrome, celiac disease, and food intolerances can make alcohol's effects on the gut much more noticeable, and a doctor can help sort out what's going on.

## Does Drinking Less Change Your Morning-After Bathroom Trips?

Yes, and this is the most reliable fix. Alcohol's effects on the gut depend heavily on dose. Fewer drinks, a slower pace, food in your stomach before and during drinking, and water between drinks all reduce how much your gut is irritated and how dehydrated you get. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best support, and [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why eating first matters so much.

Some people also add a supplement as part of their routine. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly in animal and lab studies, with limited human data so far. There is no good evidence that DHM settles your gut or changes your bathroom trips, and it doesn't replace drinking less, eating, and hydrating. If you want to try it as part of a broader plan, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands honestly.

## The Bottom Line

- Pooping can make you feel better when you're hungover, mainly because it stimulates your vagus nerve and relieves an irritated, bloated gut.
- It does **not** remove alcohol or acetaldehyde from your body. Your liver handles almost all of that, and the alcohol was absorbed long before it could reach your colon.
- Alcohol often causes loose, urgent stools by speeding up your gut and interfering with water absorption. Late-night food, beer, sugary mixers, and caffeine add to it.
- Diarrhea makes dehydration worse, so replace fluids and salts.
- Don't force it with laxatives, detox teas, or pots of coffee.
- Be careful of lightheadedness on the toilet. Don't strain, and stand up slowly.
- See a doctor for blood, black tarry stools, severe belly pain, diarrhea longer than two days, or fainting.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does pooping help a hangover?**

It can make you feel better for a while, but it doesn't cure the hangover. A bowel movement can stimulate the vagus nerve, which can briefly relax you, and it relieves cramping and bloating in a gut that alcohol has irritated. It doesn't remove alcohol or speed up your recovery. Water, food, rest, and time are what actually help.

**Why do I feel so much better after I poop when I'm hungover?**

A few reasons combine. Having a bowel movement can stimulate the vagus nerve, which can briefly lower your heart rate and create a feeling of relief or calm. Emptying an irritated, gassy gut also eases cramping and nausea. And you often go after drinking water, eating, or having coffee, which help on their own.

**Can you poop out alcohol?**

No. Alcohol is absorbed quickly through your stomach and small intestine into your blood, long before it would reach your colon. Your liver breaks down the vast majority of it, and a small amount leaves through breath, urine, and sweat. Stool isn't a meaningful way your body gets rid of alcohol, so pooping won't sober you up or lower your blood alcohol.

**Why do I poop so much after drinking alcohol?**

Alcohol can speed up how fast food and fluid move through your gut, interfere with how your intestines absorb water and salts, and irritate the gut lining. That leads to frequent, loose stools. Beer, sugary mixers, caffeine, and greasy late-night food can make it worse. It usually settles within a day.

**Is it bad to have diarrhea with a hangover?**

It's usually not dangerous on its own, but it does make dehydration worse because you lose water and salts. Drink fluids with some sodium and sugar, such as an electrolyte drink or broth, and eat bland food. See a doctor if it lasts more than two days, if you see blood or black stools, or if you can't keep fluids down.

**Why am I constipated after drinking?**

Dehydration from alcohol makes your colon pull more water out of stool, leaving it hard and difficult to pass. Disrupted sleep, skipped meals, and a low-fiber night of snacks add to it. Drinking water steadily, eating some fiber, and walking around usually help within a day or two. Avoid strong laxatives unless a doctor or pharmacist suggests one.

**Can you faint on the toilet when hungover?**

It's uncommon, but it can happen. Bearing down can stimulate the vagus nerve and drop your heart rate and blood pressure, and dehydration and alcohol make that more likely. Don't strain, stand up slowly, and if you feel lightheaded, stay seated with your head lowered. If you faint and hit your head, have chest pain, or it happens more than once, get medical care.

**Should I drink coffee to help me poop when hungover?**

Coffee does stimulate the colon for many people, but making yourself poop won't cure a hangover. One cup is usually fine if you drink coffee regularly. Several cups on an empty, irritated stomach can worsen nausea, anxiety, and a racing heart, and it won't replace water.
